Professor Albright, a man whose life revolved around the precise alignment of facts and the immutable laws of physics, had long since retired to his study for the evening. The gas lamp hissed softly, casting a warm, steady glow upon his worn leather chair and the towering shelves of books. He was engrossed in a particularly dense treatise on celestial mechanics, a subject that offered him comforting order amidst the world’s unpredictable clamour. It was past midnight, and the house was utterly still, save for the occasional settling creak of ancient timbers.

Then, he heard it, a faint rustle, distinct from the rustle of turning pages or the scratch of his own pen. He paused, his brow furrowed, and listened. Nothing. He returned to his work, but the silence seemed to hold a new quality, a tautness that had not been there moments before. A breath, perhaps, close by. His hand, however steady on the page, felt an unaccountable chill, a sensation he attributed to the late hour and an overlooked draught.

His eyes strayed from the text, drawn to the mahogany desk across the room, where his own inkwell stood beside a stack of fresh parchment. As he watched, a pen, a silver-nibbed instrument he cherished, lifted itself from its rest. It hung there, shimmering faintly in the lamplight, a full six inches above the polished wood. Albright blinked, then blinked again, convinced his eyes played tricks, tired from strain. Yet the pen remained suspended, an impossible thing, defying gravity and logic with an unsettling grace.

“Indeed, it is no trick,” a low voice articulated, a voice devoid of body, seeming to emanate from the very air before him. “Your senses are quite accurate, Professor.”

Albright’s pipe, which he had been raising to his lips, clattered against the desk, sending a shower of embers across his papers. He swore under his breath, a rare lapse in his decorum. He stared at the spot where the voice had seemed to hover, his face paling. No one else was in the house; that much he knew with absolute certainty.

“Who, who is there?” he demanded, his own voice a raspy whisper, barely audible above the hiss of the lamp. He snatched up the brass poker from beside the fireplace, his knuckles white around the cold metal.

“A rather unusual visitor, I confess,” replied the voice, which now seemed to have shifted, sounding closer to the bookshelf behind him. Albright spun around, the poker held defensively. He saw nothing, only the orderly rows of spines, their titles glimmering in the soft light. “You see, Professor, I have something of a dimensional issue.”

Albright’s mind, accustomed to grappling with complex equations and theoretical physics, found itself at a profound loss. His scientific training screamed charlatanry; his every instinct screamed impossibility. Yet the pen, now gently swaying, and the voice, so undeniably present, could not be dismissed. “Dimensional issue,” he repeated slowly, tasting the words, trying to make sense of the nonsensical. “Are you suggesting, you are not entirely here?”

“Precisely so,” the voice affirmed, a note of weariness underlying its ethereal tone. “Or, rather, I am here, but not quite in the manner you expect. It is a most inconvenient state of affairs, I assure you.” A small, leather-bound volume on the shelf, a first edition of Kepler, slid horizontally a few inches, then dropped with a soft thud onto the floor. Albright flinched, his heart hammering against his ribs. He gripped the poker tighter.

“What, what do you want?” he asked, a tremor in his voice he could not suppress. His skepticism warred with a rising tide of primal fear. This was beyond the scope of his known universe.

“Warmth, primarily,” the voice replied, and now it seemed to be near the fireplace, an invisible presence settling itself into the empty armchair. The cushion of the chair noticeably compressed, a subtle depression appearing where an invisible weight had settled. Albright gaped, his mouth agape. “And perhaps a measure of understanding, Professor. You, a man of science, might grasp the intricacies of my predicament, however unbelievable it may seem.”

“Unbelievable is an understatement,” Albright muttered, lowering the poker slightly, though still holding it ready. He watched the indentation in the armchair, mesmerised by its impossible reality. “This, this defies every known law of nature, every principle I have dedicated my life to studying.”

“Indeed it does,” the voice conceded, a hint of something like dry humour in its tone. “Or perhaps it simply reveals a few laws you have yet to discover. I am not a ghost, Professor, nor a spirit. I am, for want of a better term, a man. A man who, through a series of rather unfortunate experiments, has found himself, dislocated. Displaced, one might say, from his proper locus in space-time.”

Albright found himself staring, not at the chair, but at the empty space above it. The air shimmered, or so he imagined, in the lamplight. A shiver ran down his spine, not entirely from fear, but from a profound intellectual shock. His mind, trained for inquiry, began to stir beyond the initial paralysis. “Experiments, you say?” he questioned, his voice now steadier, a spark of scientific curiosity overriding his terror. “What kind of experiments could possibly lead to such a condition?”

“The kind that one undertakes in pursuit of, ultimate theory,” the voice articulated, a sigh, or the suggestion of one, seeming to disturb the air. “But that is a long tale, Professor, and I confess I am quite chilled, and rather weary. My state, you see, is not conducive to maintaining warmth, nor substance, without great effort. May I beg the indulgence of your fire? And perhaps, a blanket? And a strong cup of tea, if it is not too much trouble. I have not felt the warmth of a hearth in what feels like an eternity.”

Albright stood motionless for a moment, absorbing the request. A disembodied man, a man of science, asking for tea and a blanket. The sheer absurdity of it struck him, and a nervous, almost hysterical laugh escaped his lips. He ran a hand through his thinning grey hair. “A blanket,” he repeated, shaking his head. “And tea. For a dimensional anomaly.” He walked to the fireplace, poked the embers back to life, and then, with a strange sense of resignation, headed towards the hall closet where the spare throws were kept. The world, he mused, was far stranger than even he, a cosmologist, had ever dared to imagine. He returned with a thick woollen blanket. He extended it towards the seemingly empty armchair. It was taken from his hands, the fabric vanishing into thin air, only to reappear, draped across the depressed cushion. He heard a faint, appreciative sound, like a sigh of deep comfort.

“Thank you, Professor,” the voice said, softer now, as if settling down. “You are a man of rare composure. Most would be screaming.”

“I may yet,” Albright muttered, turning towards the kitchen. “But first, tea.” He felt a bizarre excitement now, a thrill of scientific discovery mixed with the lingering unease. His understanding of the universe had just profoundly shifted; the laws of nature had, in a single, impossible evening, acquired a thrilling, terrifying new clause. He returned with a steaming mug of tea, and extended it into the air above the armchair. It was taken, and he heard the faint sound of liquid being sipped, a sound that, however impossible, was undeniably real.
